title: Long USO — WTI $90 Re-Entry on Trump Civilian Infrastructure Ultimatum + Saudi Tanker Attacks
entry: $130–136 (intraday July 23). WTI is at $90.14 — a full $10.14 above the $80 September hike trip wire documented in the prior USO opportunity (closed July 22 at Target 1). The conflict has escalated materially since that trade: Trump issued a civilian infrastructure ultimatum on July 22 (first-ever explicit target set on Iranian civil energy grid), followed by Saudi tanker attacks overnight, bringing a new risk tier — Gulf state energy infrastructure as a direct target — that was not priced in the prior trade. This is a structurally higher-severity phase with distinct new catalysts; enter the re-entry position at market on July 23 open or on any intraday dip to $130. Do not initiate above $136.
stop_loss: $116 daily close (~12.8% below $133 reference) — at $116, WTI has fallen back below $78, implying that (1) a ceasefire has been announced AND Hormuz commercial throughput has recovered above 70% of normal capacity (same condition that invalidated the prior trade), removing the entire supply-disruption premium; OR (2) Trump walks back the civilian infrastructure ultimatum after diplomatic intervention (G7 emergency communiqué or UN Security Council resolution); OR (3) Saudi Arabia confirms tanker attacks were by non-state actors without IRGC direction, defusing the Gulf state escalation tier. Below $116, the escalation thesis at this severity level is broken.
targets: $145 — WTI sustains above $93 for 3 consecutive sessions; August CPI loading effect confirmed (WTI at $90+ for 10+ trading days before August BLS cutoff embeds 1.0–1.3 ppt of energy into August CPI headline); September hike probability moves to 85%+; USO +9.0% from $133 reference; cover 40% in weeks 1–2

$158 — Iranian civilian infrastructure strike executed by US forces (Trump ultimatum acted upon); WTI spikes to $98–102 on civilian grid targeting signal; Brent above $104; Gulf state shipping insurance exclusion-zone costs spike to 300%+ of baseline; USO +18.8%; cover 40% of remaining

$175 — Full Hormuz-closure scenario with Gulf state infrastructure targeting: WTI above $110; Iran formally retaliates against Saudi Aramco facilities or UAE oil infrastructure; US deploys second carrier strike group and establishes no-transit zone; USO approaches all-time high territory; +31.6%; hold final 20%
risk_reward: 1:2.5 to Target 3 from $133 reference (risk $17; T3 reward $42)
catalyst: Three new catalysts since the prior USO trade closed at Target 1 ($127) on July 22: (1) Trump issued a civilian infrastructure ultimatum on July 22 — the first explicit threat to target Iranian civilian energy grid assets, representing a qualitative escalation beyond the previous military-base and IRGC strike pattern; (2) Saudi tanker attacks occurred overnight July 22–23, introducing Gulf state energy infrastructure as a new conflict front; (3) WTI reached $90.14 on July 22 — already $10.14 above the September hike trip wire — embedding a new, higher oil-price baseline into August CPI before the BLS collection cutoff (approximately July 25–August 5). The WTI-to-CPI loading effect is now mechanically in motion for August 12 release.
thesis:
The prior USO trade (July 14–22) captured the initial Hormuz re-pricing from $79.56 to $127 on USO (+7.8%). That trade was based on WTI moving from $79.56 toward the $80 September hike trip wire. The re-entry thesis is structurally different and more severe: WTI is now at $90.14, already past the trip wire, and the conflict has escalated to a qualitatively new tier — civilian infrastructure targeting — that the prior trade did not anticipate.

The civilian infrastructure ultimatum changes the probability distribution of outcomes. The prior escalation was military-on-military (IRGC vs. CENTCOM, targeting bases and naval assets). Trump's July 22 ultimatum is the first explicit threat to Iran's civilian energy grid — its oil export terminals, power generation facilities, and pipeline infrastructure. If acted upon, this represents a precedent-setting escalation that would trigger Iranian retaliation against Gulf state civilian infrastructure (Saudi Aramco processing facilities, UAE oil terminals). The prior USO trade's bull case (IRGC naval interdiction) mapped to a $149 USO target; the re-entry bull case (civilian grid targeting + Gulf state infrastructure retaliation) maps to a qualitatively higher severity tier with $175 as the blue-sky level.

The WTI-to-CPI mechanism is now in active motion. With WTI at $90.14, the August CPI calculation (BLS data collection cutoff approximately July 25–August 5, release August 12) will mechanically embed 1.0–1.3 percentage points of energy contribution — turning what would have been a 3.8% July CPI toward 4.8–5.0% in August. That trajectory is now largely locked in regardless of what happens to WTI in the next two weeks. The September FOMC (September 16) will be presented with an August CPI of approximately 4.8–5.0% and a WTI price that will remain elevated as long as the conflict persists. September hike probability is already at 71% (per this morning's briefing) and will move toward 85%+ on the August 12 CPI release.

USO remains the correct vehicle for this thesis: it provides pure WTI crude oil exposure without the equity-specific risk (earnings, capex, dividend coverage) that XOM and XLE carry. XOM's Target 1 was hit at $152 on July 22 and has now been closed; the energy exposure in the book should be via the commodity itself, not the equity, for the continuation of the Iran/Hormuz trade. The 3% position size matches the prior USO trade — appropriate for a macro geopolitical bet with defined stop loss.

The counter-party argues: (1) the civilian infrastructure ultimatum is a negotiating tactic, not a genuine targeting plan — Trump has issued ultimatums before without following through, and the G7 or UN may constrain escalation; (2) Saudi tanker attacks, if confirmed as IRGC-directed, could actually accelerate a diplomatic resolution as Gulf states pressure both the US and Iran toward de-escalation to protect their own assets; (3) at WTI $90, the demand-destruction signal from higher energy costs is beginning to show in freight and industrial data, which may self-limit the oil price before the $98–102 range implied in Target 2. These are valid near-term risks — the stop at $116 defines the maximum loss.
bull_case: Trump's civilian infrastructure ultimatum is acted upon within 10 days (US strikes Iranian oil export terminals or power generation nodes); Iran retaliates against Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing facility or UAE offshore platforms; WTI spikes to $105+; USO reaches $158–$175 within 3 weeks. Saudi Arabia and UAE declare force majeure on oil export commitments, triggering a global supply shock of 5–8% of daily crude production. This is the scenario where the conflict moves from geopolitical risk premium to actual supply disruption.
bear_case: G7 emergency meeting produces a diplomatic framework; Trump treats civilian infrastructure ultimatum as a successful deterrent (Iran backs down on tanker interdiction); back-channel US-Iran communications confirmed within 5 days; WTI reverses from $90 toward $80–82 as the civilian-targeting escalation fear premium deflates. USO pulls back to $118–$122, approaching but not triggering the $116 stop. The prior ceasefire in June 2026 demonstrated how rapidly WTI can retrace when diplomatic resolution appears credible.
invalidation: $116 daily close (full escalation-premium deflation implied); OR ceasefire announced AND Hormuz commercial throughput confirmed above 70% normal (WTI falls below $78 immediately); OR Trump explicitly walks back civilian infrastructure ultimatum in a formal statement (White House briefing or executive order); OR Saudi tanker attacks confirmed as non-state actors without IRGC direction and Saudi Arabia publicly accepts that conclusion; OR WTI falls below $82 for two consecutive sessions regardless of reason (structural demand-destruction signal)
